messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 62
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Potter
- Trauma Type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
- Pcl5: 60

He was sixty-two years old when his son died. That’s how he thinks of it now, even though it’s been seven years. His son, Caleb, was twenty-eight, a woodworker, and had been helping him unload a kiln one Saturday afternoon. A shelf gave way—old, warped, unnoticed—and the stoneware fell. Not the pots. The shelf itself, the heavy wooden bracket that held the whole top row. It landed across Caleb’s chest and neck. He died before the ambulance arrived. His wife, Marie, was calling 911 while he knelt in the shards, trying to lift the bracket. He couldn’t. It weighed more than he’d ever imagined.

In the months after, he kept working. It’s what he knew. He would go to the studio—the same small building behind their house—and stand at the wheel, but his hands wouldn’t center the clay. They’d push too hard, or not enough. The walls of the pots would collapse. He’d scrape the mess into a bucket and start again. He didn’t tell Marie how often he saw the bracket falling, how the sound of cracking wood would hit him without warning. She was grieving too. They didn’t talk much.

Now, at sixty-two, his days have a pattern. He wakes early, before light, as he always did. But he lies in bed for an hour, sometimes longer, because getting up means entering the day where Caleb is still dead. He feels the weight of that fact in his chest, a physical pressure, as if the bracket is pressing on him too. He has stopped going to the studio regularly. When he does go, he works on small pieces—cups, bowls, nothing too large. He used to make tall vases and sculpted forms. Now he can’t trust the kiln. He’ll check and recheck the firing temperature, even though nothing has gone wrong since. He once spent an entire day loading and unloading the same kiln, unable to settle on a temperature setting. Marie found him in the dark, opening and closing the door.

He avoids the back corner of the studio where the shelf was. He’s never repaired or replaced it. He keeps that area stacked with empty buckets, a kind of barricade. He tells himself he’ll get to it, but he doesn’t. When the phone rings unexpectedly, he flinches. When he hears a loud crash in the house—Marie dropping a pan—his heart pounds and his hands go cold. He has to sit down. He doesn’t tell her this. She has started to ask him if he’s okay, and he just nods.

At night, he has dreams where Caleb is alive but unreachable—standing at the other end of a long room, or on a stage, and he can’t get to him. He wakes with a start, believing for a moment that he is still twenty-eight and the day is still unbroken. Then the real morning comes. He thinks about Caleb’s laugh, the way he would rub his thumb across the rim of a newly thrown bowl, the sawdust in his hair. He tries to hold onto those memories, but they slip away, replaced by the image of the shelf falling. He worries he is forgetting his son. That worry is another weight.

Yesterday, a young woman came to the studio to buy a mug. She said, “Your work has a kind of quiet strength.” He thanked her and handed her the mug. His hands were trembling slightly. He didn’t know if she noticed. He used to love talking to customers about his process. Now he wants them to leave. He wants to go back inside, where no one sees him.

He is not sure why he started seeing me. Marie made the call. He came because she asked. He sits in the chair and tells these things slowly, his voice flat, his eyes on his hands. He says, “I don’t know if this is normal for grief.” He doesn’t use the word trauma. He doesn’t know that the bracket still falls every day in his mind, and that he is still trying to lift it.
